doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: The bass's responsibility, Ray Brown's advice and never stopping
summary: Lessons from the Seattle experience, Ray Brown on keeping the bass up front, and the bassist's power to make or break a band.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Did that experience with the singer that time find its way into your teaching?

Oh absolutely. That’s where those statements come from of stop leaning on other people to make you sound good. Because that’s what bass players tend to do. And most people say, “Oh I didn’t know a bass could do that.” Well the bass is not doing that, the bass is just a conduit of what the brain is doing, really. But people don’t hear that. I mean the bass is — Ray Brown used to tell me, he says, “Well, you know, keep the bass up front. We know we’re in the back, but the bass is always up front.” And he says, “You be conscious of how you project your bass line.” And he says, “When it’s really good, if the saxophone player or the trumpet player are not really taking care of business, the listener’s ears are coming right past them, because of the way that you’re sounding.” I said, “Really?” But we have that ability to destroy, we have that power to either make great or break the ensemble. Just like that. And so to me that’s a big responsibility. And I think a lot of people don’t really know that. I mean I can destroy a group better than anybody. I mean drummers think they can do that too, but everybody in the group has that ability, but I think I can do it better, because everything really resonates from the bass.

That’s a great statement. You can put that on your resume. You know it’s such a different thing for a saxophone player, which I play. If you half know a tune you probably can get through it. You can play the melody and then you can listen to the guys do the harmony, and you can get through it. But you guys, you can’t stop concentrating I guess.

You can’t stop. You can’t stop. I mean if I stop while you were playing you’d lean around and say, “What the hell is wrong with you?” And drummers can’t stop. They shouldn’t stop. Why are you going to stop? So if you’re not sure of what you’re doing, but you still can’t stop, so you’ve got to figure it out while you’re still in motion. And the quicker you do it, everybody’s happy.
